subject: LAW
courseTitle: Federalism in Action: The Doctrines and Constitutional Provisions That Govern Federal-State Battles
courseDescr: Clashes between the states and the federal government are an inherent feature of our Nation's federalist structure. These disagreements, which have become more common in recent years, often give rise to high-profile, politically charged cases. (See, e.g., West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022) ; Trump v. Hawaii, 585 U.S. 667 (2018); Biden v. Nebraska, 143 S. Ct. 2355 (2023); Arizona v. United States, 567 U.S. 387 (2012); United States v. Illinois, 25-cv-1285 (N.D. Ill.); United States v. Vermont, 25-cv-00463 (D. Vt.)). To resolve these disputes, courts have developed many important legal doctrines, including federal preemption, anti-commandeering, federal common law, the Dormant Commerce Clause, and many more. This course will examine these doctrines as well as the seminal cases interpreting the Supremacy Clause, Commerce Clause, Spending Clause, and the various other constitutional provisions that establish the boundaries of federal and state power. The goal of this class is to better understand the jurisprudence that has developed to keep the federal and state governments within their respective spheres of authority. This class will be especially valuable for those interested in clerking in the federal courts, working as a litigator in the Department of Justice or a state solicitor general's office, and/or learning how many of our today's most contentious cases are likely to be resolved. Elements used in grading: Attendance, Class participation, Exam.

subject: LAW
courseDescr: At 19 percent of the total population, Latinos are currently, in percentage terms, the largest single racial minority group in United States history. As a result, more and more of the law will develop in the future through cases that emanate from and involve members of the Latino community. This course explores how the United States legal system has grappled with the specific concerns and discrimination issues faced by the Latino community. This course will review and critique cases in multiple areas, including Census, consumer protection, education, employment, immigration, jury exclusion, racial classification, and voting rights. This course will explore current issues faced by Latinos in light of contemporary threats to the rule of law. Elements used in grading: Attendance, class participation, short response papers, open book exam.

subject: LAW
courseDescr: This seminar will examine current research by lawyers and economists on a variety of topics in law and economics. Several sessions of the seminar will consist of an invited speaker, usually from another university, who will discuss his or her current research. Representative of these sessions have been discussions of compensation for government regulations and takings, liability rules for controlling accidents, the definition of markets in antitrust analysis, the role of the government as a controlling shareholder, and optimal drug patent length. Special Instructions: You may write a series of short commentaries on the guest speakers' papers, of which there will be four. Students electing this option will be graded on a Mandatory Pass/Restricted Credit/Fail basis and receive 2 units of credit. Alternatively, you may write a single research paper on a law and economics topic of your choice. This will satisfy the Law School's Research requirement. These papers will be graded on an Honors/Pass/Restricted Credit/Fail basis. (You may write a single longer paper for two quarters if you enroll in the Seminar in the Winter as well.). After the term begins, students accepted into the course can transfer from section (01) into section (02), which meets the R requirement, with consent of the instructor. There is no formal economics prerequisite to take this seminar, though students doing the longer research papers typically have some prior training in economics. Students may take both Law and Economics Seminar (A) and Law and Economics Seminar (W) in either order (neither is a prerequisite for the other). Elements used in grading: Four commentaries or one research paper. Special note: Professor Polinsky will be the principal instructor, with Professor Donohue participating mainly when there are guest speakers. Cross-listed with Economics (ECON 354). CONSENT APPLICATION: To apply for this course, students must complete and submit a Consent Application Form available on the SLS website (https://law.stanford.edu/education/courses/consent-of-instructor-forms/). See Consent Application Form for instructions and submission deadline.

subject: LAW
courseDescr: As a lawyer, you will probably negotiate more than you do anything else. You will negotiate not just over cases, but any time that you need something that you cannot get alone. You will negotiate with your boss, your clients, your paralegal, and all of their counterparts (plus the lawyers) on the other side. You will negotiate with "the system" whether it is the court, the government, the structure of society, or the law. You will also continue to negotiate with your family, your friends, and yourself. This course is designed to: (1) develop your understanding of negotiation, and your awareness of yourself as a negotiator; (2) give you some tools and concepts for analyzing and preparing for negotiations; (3) enhance your negotiating skills through frequent role plays, reflection, and feedback; and (4) teach you how to keep learning from your own negotiation experience. In addition to negotiation skills and theory (including interviewing, counseling, negotiation, fact analysis, legal analysis, and collaboration), you will be introduced to issues of representation, ethics, and the place of negotiation in our legal system. The Negotiation Seminar is an intense, interactive course. We will require weekly preparation of readings, simulations, and written assignments. Basically, you will learn by reading about specific research and doing simulated negotiations -- figuring out with the rest of the class what works and what does not, writing about what you're learning, and trying again. Because participation in the simulations is central to the course, attendance at all classes is required. Since we will begin our simulation exercises on the first day of class, all students who are interested in taking the course (whether enrolled or on the wait-list) need to be present for the first class. (Students who are not present will be dropped from the class or waiting list unless they have made previous arrangements with the instructor.) Add-drop decisions need to be resolved at the first class. Elements used in grading: Class participation, attendance and written assignments.

subject: INDE
courseTitle: Intro to Specialty Career Selection: Exploring Residency Specialty Selection with Career Advisors
courseDescr: Are you intimidated by the number of specialty choices out there? Do you want to feel more confident when answering the dreaded question, "What kind of doctor do you want to be?" The School of Medicine Center for Specialty Career Advising is offering a 2-quarter seminar series highlighting the different specialty career choices offered for your residency training. We recognize that undergraduates and medical students may have a general idea of what field of medicine they might be interested in pursuing, but often aren't exposed to the vast number of choices until later in their clinical years. This series will feature 20 different and popular specialties. Each week, we will highlight a different specialty through a seminar led by the Specialty Career Advisor (SCA) in that field of medicine. Each SCA is carefully selected as an expert and mentor in that field and will provide you with an overview of what to expect should you choose that specialty. Each overview will also provide a next steps framework to learn more about the field with ample time for Q&A. There is no better time to start exploring than now! This series is a Pass-Fail attendance only course.

subject: AFRICAAM
courseDescr: Print on Purpose is where designing forward while looking back at the legacy of print for social change meets in an immersive design space. Join us for a rigorous course that probes the intersection of visual expression and freedom of speech. We dissect the role print has played as a driver of social change, covering media ranging from newspapers, zines, posters, pamphlets, vinyl album covers, stickers, to lawn signs. Print on Purpose is an introduction to visual communications tools and processes that impact the way our work is produced and received. It's about experimentation with typography, drawing, and imagery, and inevitably rolling up your sleeves and producing prints. This course emphasizes the importance of DIY production methods and works with students to utilize the resources available to them to produce printed materials. Critiques will be a fundamental part of each project, as will the incorporation of feedback. You will be expected to participate in evaluating your own work and that of your peers in group settings.

subject: ARCHLGY
courseTitle: Muwekma(CEL) Traditional Ecological Knowledge(TEK) Native Plant Garden Field Project
courseDescr: Indigenous Ecological Knowledge refers to the Indigenous knowledge related to human beliefs, practices and experiences embedded in specific locations. There are multiple versions of such knowledge based on the unique relationships of individual communities with a focus on California Native Communities (Specifically the Muwekma Ohlone tribe). We will explore environmental justice movements, sacred lands and medicines, climate change adaptation, resiliency, the effects of colonization on Indigenous food systems and ecological restoration. We will examine the ways in which Native Peoples responded and adapted to settler colonialism, dispossession, cultural genocide, and the rise of the 'Ranchosphere' in California.  We will foreground the voices of Indigenous scholars and scientists. This course will allow students interested in working with the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe to engage in Community Based Participatory Research (CBPR) through (CEL) Community Engaged Learning. This CARDINAL COURSE  draws from the knowledge and support provided by The HAAS Center. NOTE: Native Am 112 can be taken for up to 3 units and is not repeatable. Native Am 12 is a repeatable project-based lab that can be taken for 1-2 units. No more than 5 units of Native Am 12/112 can be counted toward a CCSRE major or minor.

subject: ARCHLGY
courseTitle: Archaeological Field Methods: Excavating Campus Histories at Frenchman's Lake
courseDescr: This hands-on course introduces students to archaeological field methods through active participation in the excavation of the multi-layered Frenchman's Lake site on the Stanford campus. Students will gain practical experience while investigating a deposit from Stanford campus dating to the early 20th century. Students will be trained in a range of core archaeological techniques, including survey, mapping, testing, and excavation, with an emphasis on digging, recording units and features, and illustrating stratigraphic profiles. The site's rich historical layers - ranging from 19th-century European settlement to early Stanford student recreation and the creation of a public park - offer a dynamic setting to explore archaeological methods. Beyond technical training, the course encourages critical inquiry into how archaeology can illuminate everyday life, institutional histories, and the material legacy of the modern university. Open to all, no experience required.

subject: ARTHIST
courseTitle: Otherized and Organized: The Politicization of Indigeneity in Colonial Latin America
courseDescr: This course focuses on Indigenous visual, material, and cultural production of early colonial Latin America (Viceroyalty of Peru and Viceroyalty of New Spain) from the mid-1500s through the mid-1700s, with some content on the very late precontact period before colonization. During this period, Indigenous Latin American peoples experienced dramatic changes to their autonomy and lifeways, with implications for their languages, social organization, and relationship to the landscape. The class will review artifacts, texts, and other cultural expressions to bring forward the complexity of cultural clash between various Indigenous and European actors and to sort through how material and cultural value--and changing value--factored into questions of political and social order. Study of cross-cultural shifts incorporates emerging discourses on race, ethnicity, and social justice. In this scope, we will address discourses and debates regarding difference, alterity, the hybrid, the transcultural, etc., and analyze how visual and material culture examples bring forward Indigenous identities as perceived and politicized in relation to questions of self and other, with attention mainly to Indigenous creators and audiences but also their European counterparts. Furthermore, a component of the class will include contemporary artworks that reflect on the reverberations of colonization of the Americas.

subject: ARTHIST
courseDescr: What impact do images have on our reading of a text? How do words influence our understanding of images or our reading of pictures? What makes a visual interpretation of written words or a verbal rendering of an image successful? These questions will guide our investigation of the manifold connections between words and images in this course on intermediality and the relations and interrelations between writing and art from classical antiquity to the present. Readings and discussions will include such topics as the life and afterlife in word and image of Ovid's "Metamorphoses," Dante's "Divine Comedy," Ludovico Ariosto's "Orlando Furioso," and John Milton's "Paradise Lost;" the writings and creative production of poet-artists Michelangelo Buonarroti, William Blake, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti; innovations in and correspondences between literature and art in the modern period, from symbolism in the nineteenth century through the flourishing of European avant-garde movements in the twentieth century.

subject: ITALIAN
courseDescr: What impact do images have on our reading of a text? How do words influence our understanding of images or our reading of pictures? What makes a visual interpretation of written words or a verbal rendering of an image successful? These questions will guide our investigation of the manifold connections between words and images in this course on intermediality and the relations and interrelations between writing and art from classical antiquity to the present. Readings and discussions will include such topics as the life and afterlife in word and image of Ovid's "Metamorphoses," Dante's "Divine Comedy," Ludovico Ariosto's "Orlando Furioso," and John Milton's "Paradise Lost;" the writings and creative production of poet-artists Michelangelo Buonarroti, William Blake, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti; innovations in and correspondences between literature and art in the modern period, from symbolism in the nineteenth century through the flourishing of European avant-garde movements in the twentieth century.

subject: NATIVEAM
courseTitle: Muwekma(CEL) Traditional Ecological Knowledge(TEK) Native Plant Garden Field Project
courseDescr: Indigenous Ecological Knowledge refers to the Indigenous knowledge related to human beliefs, practices and experiences embedded in specific locations. There are multiple versions of such knowledge based on the unique relationships of individual communities with a focus on California Native Communities (Specifically the Muwekma Ohlone tribe). We will explore environmental justice movements, sacred lands and medicines, climate change adaptation, resiliency, the effects of colonization on Indigenous food systems and ecological restoration. We will examine the ways in which Native Peoples responded and adapted to settler colonialism, dispossession, cultural genocide, and the rise of the 'Ranchosphere' in California.  We will foreground the voices of Indigenous scholars and scientists. This course will allow students interested in working with the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe to engage in Community Based Participatory Research (CBPR) through (CEL) Community Engaged Learning. This CARDINAL COURSE  draws from the knowledge and support provided by The HAAS Center. NOTE: Native Am 112 can be taken for up to 3 units and is not repeatable. Native Am 12 is a repeatable project-based lab that can be taken for 1-2 units. No more than 5 units of Native Am 12/112 can be counted toward a CCSRE major or minor.

subject: NATIVEAM
courseTitle: Otherized and Organized: The Politicization of Indigeneity in Colonial Latin America
courseDescr: This course focuses on Indigenous visual, material, and cultural production of early colonial Latin America (Viceroyalty of Peru and Viceroyalty of New Spain) from the mid-1500s through the mid-1700s, with some content on the very late precontact period before colonization. During this period, Indigenous Latin American peoples experienced dramatic changes to their autonomy and lifeways, with implications for their languages, social organization, and relationship to the landscape. The class will review artifacts, texts, and other cultural expressions to bring forward the complexity of cultural clash between various Indigenous and European actors and to sort through how material and cultural value--and changing value--factored into questions of political and social order. Study of cross-cultural shifts incorporates emerging discourses on race, ethnicity, and social justice. In this scope, we will address discourses and debates regarding difference, alterity, the hybrid, the transcultural, etc., and analyze how visual and material culture examples bring forward Indigenous identities as perceived and politicized in relation to questions of self and other, with attention mainly to Indigenous creators and audiences but also their European counterparts. Furthermore, a component of the class will include contemporary artworks that reflect on the reverberations of colonization of the Americas.

subject: POLISCI
courseTitle: AI Policy Development: Leveraging Social Science to Ensure Responsible Generative AI
courseDescr: How should frontier AI companies decide what their models may enable, who should have access, and when the state or public should have a say? In this policy practicum, students work as product-policy advisors to a frontier AI company, drawing on social science research, political theory, and historical cases to develop feasible recommendations for real AI policy problems. The course treats decisions about model behavior, access, deployment, privacy, safety, and enforcement as a form of governance that allocates power among companies, citizens, and the state. Historical cases including the printing press, nuclear technology, railroads, radio, pharmaceutical regulation, algorithmic trading, and the Crypto Wars illuminate recurring dilemmas that students apply to contemporary AI products. Students produce policy memos and participate in a multi-stakeholder simulation based on a current AI product-policy question. This course is a Capstone course for the Political Science Major. Enrollment in the class is prioritized for Political Science Seniors. Completion of POLISCI 1: The Science of Politics is required prior to enrollment.

subject: PSYC
courseTitle: Wellbeing on The Farm [Skills Training for Emotional Problem Solving in College and Beyond]
courseDescr: This course teaches skills to cultivate wellbeing and resilience in the face of common stressors and difficulties. Resilience is not only about your ability to adapt positively in the face of adverse or challenging circumstances (survive), but also about learning the skills, strategies, and routines that help you live a fulfilling and successful life (thrive).   PSYC 151: Wellbeing on The Farm goes beyond traditional self-care by training students to apply systematic, evidence-based inquiry methods to the daily social realities of life at Stanford - including academic stress, social life, residential communities, and team sports. Drawing on behavioral science research, the curriculum adapts the core modules of Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) - Mindfulness, Distress Tolerance, Emotion Regulation, and Interpersonal Effectiveness - by stripping away clinical components to create a universal resiliency curriculum. Students will examine how these skills function as tools for navigating group dynamics and campus culture. By treating their lived experiences as a primary data set, students use quantitative and qualitative empirical methods to analyze patterns in human behavior and institutional structures. The course equips students with a framework for understanding wellbeing as a set of shared social interactions. Our goal is for students to develop a personalized resilience toolbox grounded in a critical appraisal of social scientific evidence, enabling them to both survive and thrive within the Stanford ecosystem and beyond.

subject: SLAVIC
courseTitle: Yugoslavia and the Literature of Freedom
courseDescr: The country of Yugoslavia existed for less than a century, and in that brief time, it developed a novel socialist system and culture that decisively broke with Stalin's Soviet bloc; formed connections with India, Indonesia, Egypt, Ghana, and other countries across Asia, Africa, and Latin America through the Non-Aligned Movement; and fostered some of the 20th century's most exciting and critical literature, cinema, philosophy, and art. For many observers, the legacy of Yugoslavia has been eclipsed by its violent end during the wars and genocide of the 1990s, but scholars identifying with "New Yugoslav Studies" increasingly reject the notion that ethno-nationalism and the destruction of socialist Yugoslavia are the only lens through which its significance ought to be viewed. Yugoslavia's end was no more preordained by fate than were its origins. In fact, Yugoslav literature, history, and culture provides some of the modern world's most gripping reflections upon freedom and self-determination, on both an individual and a collective scale. In this course, we will read literary masterpieces from both the short-lived interwar Kingdom of Yugoslavia (a.k.a. the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes) and the more long-lasting Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under Tito, as well as some more contemporary texts from post-Yugoslav states and writers from the former Yugoslav diaspora. Authors will include Miroslav Krleza, Ivo Andric, Mesa Selimovic, Danilo Kis, Miljenko Jergovic, Dubravka Ugresic, Masa Kolanovic, and more. Readings and discussion in English with optional Bosnian/Croatian/Montenegrin/Serbian component for those who are interested.

subject: ARCHLGY
courseTitle: Archaeological Field Methods: Excavating Campus Histories at Frenchman's Lake
courseDescr: This hands-on course introduces students to archaeological field methods through active participation in the excavation of the multi-layered Frenchman's Lake site on the Stanford campus. Students will gain practical experience while investigating a deposit from Stanford campus dating to the early 20th century. Students will be trained in a range of core archaeological techniques, including survey, mapping, testing, and excavation, with an emphasis on digging, recording units and features, and illustrating stratigraphic profiles. The site's rich historical layers - ranging from 19th-century European settlement to early Stanford student recreation and the creation of a public park - offer a dynamic setting to explore archaeological methods. Beyond technical training, the course encourages critical inquiry into how archaeology can illuminate everyday life, institutional histories, and the material legacy of the modern university. Open to all, no experience required.

courseTitle.value: Archaeological Field Methods: Excavating Campus Histories at Frenchman's Lake

courseDescr.value: This hands-on course introduces students to archaeological field methods through active participation in the excavation of the multi-layered Frenchman's Lake site on the Stanford campus. Students will gain practical experience while investigating a deposit from Stanford campus dating to the early 20th century. Students will be trained in a range of core archaeological techniques, including survey, mapping, testing, and excavation, with an emphasis on digging, recording units and features, and illustrating stratigraphic profiles. The site's rich historical layers - ranging from 19th-century European settlement to early Stanford student recreation and the creation of a public park - offer a dynamic setting to explore archaeological methods. Beyond technical training, the course encourages critical inquiry into how archaeology can illuminate everyday life, institutional histories, and the material legacy of the modern university. Open to all, no experience required.

subject: ARTHIST
courseTitle: Otherized and Organized: The Politicization of Indigeneity in Colonial Latin America
courseDescr: This course focuses on Indigenous visual, material, and cultural production of early colonial Latin America (Viceroyalty of Peru and Viceroyalty of New Spain) from the mid-1500s through the mid-1700s, with some content on the very late precontact period before colonization. During this period, Indigenous Latin American peoples experienced dramatic changes to their autonomy and lifeways, with implications for their languages, social organization, and relationship to the landscape. The class will review artifacts, texts, and other cultural expressions to bring forward the complexity of cultural clash between various Indigenous and European actors and to sort through how material and cultural value--and changing value--factored into questions of political and social order. Study of cross-cultural shifts incorporates emerging discourses on race, ethnicity, and social justice. In this scope, we will address discourses and debates regarding difference, alterity, the hybrid, the transcultural, etc., and analyze how visual and material culture examples bring forward Indigenous identities as perceived and politicized in relation to questions of self and other, with attention mainly to Indigenous creators and audiences but also their European counterparts. Furthermore, a component of the class will include contemporary artworks that reflect on the reverberations of colonization of the Americas.

subject: ARTHIST
courseDescr: What impact do images have on our reading of a text? How do words influence our understanding of images or our reading of pictures? What makes a visual interpretation of written words or a verbal rendering of an image successful? These questions will guide our investigation of the manifold connections between words and images in this course on intermediality and the relations and interrelations between writing and art from classical antiquity to the present. Readings and discussions will include such topics as the life and afterlife in word and image of Ovid's "Metamorphoses," Dante's "Divine Comedy," Ludovico Ariosto's "Orlando Furioso," and John Milton's "Paradise Lost;" the writings and creative production of poet-artists Michelangelo Buonarroti, William Blake, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti; innovations in and correspondences between literature and art in the modern period, from symbolism in the nineteenth century through the flourishing of European avant-garde movements in the twentieth century.

courseDescr: How might we apply ideas from ethical theory to contemporary issues and debates in biotechnology? This course will provide critical encounters with some of the central topics in the field of bioethics, with an emphasis on new technologies. Controversies over genetic engineering, stem cell research, reproductive technologies, and genetic testing will provide an opportunity for you to critically assess arguments and evidence. We will begin with an overview of the field and the theoretical approaches to bioethics that have been derived from philosophy. You will then have the opportunity to engage in debate and learn how to identify underlying values and how to apply ideas from ethical theory to contemporary problems.

subject: CIM
courseDescr: Health care is facing significant cross-industry challenges and opportunities created by a number of factors, including the increasing need for improved access to affordable, high-quality care; growing demand from consumers for greater control of their health and health data; the shift in focus from sick care to prevention and health optimization; aging demographics and the increased burden of chronic conditions; and new emphasis on real-world, measurable health outcomes for individuals and populations. Moreover, the delivery of health information and services is no longer tied to traditional brick and mortar hospitals and clinics: it has increasingly become "mobile," enabled by apps, sensors, wearables. Simultaneously, it has been augmented and often revolutionized by emerging digital and information technologies, as well as by the data that these technologies generate. This multifactorial transformation presents opportunities for innovation across the entire cycle of care, from wellness, to acute and chronic diseases, to care at the end of life. But how does one approach innovation in digital health to address these health care challenges while ensuring the greatest chance of success?

subject: CIM
courseDescr: Healthcare faces tremendous challenges of cost, quality and access. Technology such as AI and LLMs should help us generate solutions to these at scale, but we have yet to successfully link problems and solutions in an innovation model for the healthcare market (US and globally). This course will take on this challenge: early in the class we'll discuss some basic frameworks of the economics of technology and examine specific challenges in the healthcare system, and then we'll examine digital innovation in healthcare. Class will be a combination of case discussion and mini-lectures, and an occasional guest speaker. Concurrently, students will work individual or in teams to build a business model around innovation in healthcare.  You can bring your own problem to class, but no pressure. We'll also make a list available of problems we have identified that could provide an opportunity for innovation and newco development.

courseTitle: Perceval and the Quest for the Holy Grail
courseDescr: Beginning with Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished Conte du Graal (ca. 1180), we examine the Grail story in its inaugural vernacular form - as a text defined by incompletion, formal ambiguity, and interpretive openness. We then turn to Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (ca. 1200-1210), which transforms Chretien's enigmatic conte into an architecturally intricate exploration of guilt, grace, kinship, and knightly becoming. The seminar will also attend to the story's remarkable afterlife in literary and artistic adaptation, with students presenting an adaptation of their choosing. Readings and discussion in English.

subject: ESOLLANG
subjectDescr: English for Speakers of Other Languages
courseDescr: This course focuses on strategies for effective listening to university lectures and other academic content, such as seminars and group discussions. It extends beyond listening for main ideas and details, providing practice in identifying discourse markers common in academic settings and recognizing and accommodating implied information, hesitations, and reduced forms, such as contractions. It also covers challenging areas such as processing numbers and adapting to unfamiliar vocabulary. Listening practice is complemented by instruction in effective note-taking and study strategies to retain and review comprehended information. Additionally, the course has a significant discussion component, allowing students to interpret what they hear to develop a deeper and more critical understanding of the content and link that understanding to their spoken English production and interaction. Materials include recorded lectures from Stanford faculty and other relevant sources.

subject: GERMAN
courseTitle: Perceval and the Quest for the Holy Grail
courseDescr: Beginning with Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished Conte du Graal (ca. 1180), we examine the Grail story in its inaugural vernacular form - as a text defined by incompletion, formal ambiguity, and interpretive openness. We then turn to Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (ca. 1200-1210), which transforms Chretien's enigmatic conte into an architecturally intricate exploration of guilt, grace, kinship, and knightly becoming. The seminar will also attend to the story's remarkable afterlife in literary and artistic adaptation, with students presenting an adaptation of their choosing. Readings and discussion in English.

subject: HISTORY
courseTitle: The European Scramble for Africa: Origins and Debates
courseDescr: Why and how did Europeans claim control of 70% of African in the late nineteenth century? Students will engage with historiographical debates ranging from the national (e.g. British) to the topical (e.g. international law). Students will interrogate some of the primary sources on which debaters have rested their arguments. Key discussions include: the British occupation of Egypt; the autonomy of French colonial policy; the mystery of Germany's colonial entry; and, not least, the notorious Berlin Conference of 1884-1885.

subject: INTLPOL
courseDescr: This course aims to give students a solid understanding of the basics of modern internet technologies and an introduction to the most common types of attacks used in cybercrime and cyberwarfare. Taught by a long-time cybersecurity practitioner, each session will begin with a lecture covering the basics of an area of technology and how that technology has been misused in the past. After a short break, students will then begin a hands-on lab section, with the guidance of the instructor, where they attack a known insecure system using techniques and tools seen in the field. By the end of the course, students are expected to have a basic understanding of some of the most common offensive techniques in use today as well as the impact of AI on cybersecurity. No computer science background is required. All students must bring a Windows, Mac OS X or Linux laptop to class. This course is restricted to 25 students, with enrollment preference given to Masters in International Policy (MIP) students and other non-tech graduate students. MIP students contact jjachter@stanford.edu for an enrollment code. Other students apply at https://goto.stanford.edu/hacklab26

subject: ITALIAN
courseDescr: What impact do images have on our reading of a text? How do words influence our understanding of images or our reading of pictures? What makes a visual interpretation of written words or a verbal rendering of an image successful? These questions will guide our investigation of the manifold connections between words and images in this course on intermediality and the relations and interrelations between writing and art from classical antiquity to the present. Readings and discussions will include such topics as the life and afterlife in word and image of Ovid's "Metamorphoses," Dante's "Divine Comedy," Ludovico Ariosto's "Orlando Furioso," and John Milton's "Paradise Lost;" the writings and creative production of poet-artists Michelangelo Buonarroti, William Blake, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti; innovations in and correspondences between literature and art in the modern period, from symbolism in the nineteenth century through the flourishing of European avant-garde movements in the twentieth century.

subject: OTOHNS
courseTitle: Augmenting Human Senses: Enhancing Perception with Technology and Bioscience
courseDescr: This course will introduce the neuroscience of human sensory perception (hearing, balance, vision, smell, taste, touch) and explore avenues by which technology and bioscience will enhance and augment these human senses. Employing artificial intelligence, emerging devices with embedded sensors may afford perceptual and cognitive abilities beyond the limits of our biological systems. We will consider emerging multi-functional devices with capabilities beyond their sensory functions via connection within an ecosystem of technologies to characterize activities (e.g., physical, social), enhance safety (e.g., fall alerts, balance improvement), track health (e.g., multi-sensory biometric monitoring), enhance communication (e.g., speech enhancement, language translation, virtual assistant), augment cognition (e.g., memory, understanding), and monitor emotional wellbeing (e.g., sentiment, depression). We will also review simulated multisensory stimuli towards achieving immersive experiences with virtual and augmented reality technologies.

subject: OIT
courseDescr: This course is designed primarily, but not exclusively, for Operations, Information and Technology students of all cohorts. Students with a strong analytical background from other areas or schools are welcome. The course will focus on modeling and analysis of problems in Operations, Information Technology, AI and related areas. The course will consider both mathematical and empirical modeling, using papers and some open problems. The objective is to facilitate students' transition from learning to research.

subject: STRAMGT
courseDescr: This case-based course is offered for students who want to refine their ability to manage challenging professional conversations.  The class will focus on the preparation for and execution of role-played dialogue as well as on postmortem analysis.  Most of the respondent roles will be external to one's company, and some will be front line or mid-level people with limited educational credentials.  Broad utilization will be made of background readings and an occasional visiting expert.

subject: LAW
courseTitle: Creating Value: Private Equity, Venture Capital and Entrepreneurism
courseDescr: This course is intended for students interested in learning more about creating, building, and scaling venture capital and private equity backed companies, either directly as a principal or as an advisor. The course will take a practical and interactive approach on how venture capital and private equity companies are formed and scale, focusing on three main stages of development: (1) Formation; (2) Growth; and (3) Exit. Among the topics that will be covered are company formation (including term sheets and financing documents), scaling through M&A and organic growth, and exit events (IPO and sale). We will also cover growth equity (venture and buyout), private credit, and secondaries. The course will have guest speakers, utilize case studies, and employ a project-based approach. The course is open to Stanford Law, GSB, Engineering, and Design students. The course does not require or assume that students have taken corporate finance.  Elements used in grading: attendance, class participation, final project, and questions for, and engagement with, guest speakers. Students will be expected to have completed the readings assigned for each course and be prepared to apply them to the class discussions. This class is limited to 26 students, with an effort made to have students from SLS (by lottery) and up to five non-Law students (GSB, Engineering, and Design Schools) by consent of the instructor. Special Instructions: Students on the waitlist for the course will be admitted if spots are available on the basis of priority and degree program. Non-Law students may submit a Stanford Non-Law Student Course Add Request Form available at https://law.stanford.edu/education/courses/non-law-students/ to request consent to enroll. The class will meet the first six weeks of the quarter (Sep 22 - Oct 30).

subject: LAW
courseDescr: When federal officials seek to limit or undercut individuals' federal constitutional rights, state governments have an important role to play in protecting those rights. This course, co-taught by California's Attorney General and a California State Assembly Member, explores the role that state government officials play in protecting fundamental freedoms and expanding safety net services in times of federal retrenchment. Attention will be paid to how both litigation and state legislation function as rights-protective mechanisms. Elements used in grading: Attendance, Class Participation, Written Assignments.

subject: PAS
courseDescr: Foundations of Clinical Pharmacology introduces learners to the core principles that underpin the safe and effective use of medications in clinical practice. This course provides a framework for understanding how drugs work, how they are selected, and how they are applied across a wide range of patient care settings. Emphasis is placed on fundamental concepts such as pharmacologic mechanisms, drug interactions, and factors that influence medication safety. Foundational drug classes commonly encountered in clinical care are used to illustrate key principles. Enrollment is limited to MSPA students.

subject: PAS
courseTitle: LEAD-PA I (Leadership, Excellence, ADvocacy, and Professionalism in Action)
courseDescr:
The LEAD-PA I course introduces students to the physician assistant profession through an interdisciplinary curriculum to develop highly skilled clinicians and inspire future PA leaders. The course explores the history and evolution of the PA profession, the role of professional organizations, and the importance of advocacy in healthcare, while providing foundational guidance on graduate study strategies. 

Using the LEAD-PA framework, students develop essential professional competencies in communication, feedback, professionalism, and leadership, alongside concepts such as professional identity formation, growth mindset, resilience, and reflective practice. Structured reflection activities are introduced and continue longitudinally throughout the LEAD-PA course series. The course also orients students to the Leadership Tracks and thesis requirements, preparing them for meaningful academic and leadership engagement throughout their training. Enrollment is limited to MSPA students.

subject: PAS
courseDescr:
PAs in Health Care II equips students with the advanced clinical and procedural skills essential for success in clinical clerkships and future practice. Through immersive, hands-on training, students gain supervised experience in key bedside procedures, including suturing and wound management, gynecologic examination, point-of-care ultrasound, and advanced cardiac life support. Procedural instruction is paired with the safety, consent, and communication practices that surround each skill in real clinical settings.
The course also prompts critical engagement with the forces shaping the conditions in which patients live and seek care, including social and structural drivers of health, poverty and resource constraint, the integration of artificial intelligence into clinical practice, and the health effects of climate change. Two reflective sessions support professional identity formation and structured self-assessment of readiness for supervised practice, while clerkship preparation activities orient students to the performance and support resources available to them during the clinical year. This course is offered to students enrolled in the Master of Science in Physician Assistant Studies program only. Prerequisite: Successful completion of PAS 291

subject: PEDS
courseTitle: Writing and Storytelling Workshop for Clinical Students
courseDescr: This course is an intensive workshop for clinical students devoted to oral and written communication skills. Students receive instruction in the art and craft of storytelling for a variety of media from radio/podcast to print media. Sample of topics covered: methods for constructive self-editing; the art of interviewing; pitching creative work to agents and editors; writing craft for narrative nonfiction and personal essay; negotiating consent with subjects; communication about difficult topics; best practices for science and medical communication; and best practices for public speaking and live storytelling. The workshops are held off-campus at a local farm and are a daylong event. The Fall 2026 workshop will be on September 26, 2026 and feature two special guests. More details will be sent to registrants. Enrollment limited to 35. There will be a single two-hour follow up session.

subject: LAW
courseDescr: Mediation skills are invaluable to success in everything from negotiating commercial transactions to family interactions.  Lawyers mediate most litigated cases, even those never filed in court.  Do you want to be in the majority of people who constantly mediate, but never take a single mediation course? This course is a quick immersion in mediation advocacy, and mediation. It is intended for those who want to avoid being entirely unprepared for an essential part of legal practice and life. It is also intended for those who want to take a first step to see if mediation interests them. The two days of class will be an interactive exploration of the strategies, tactics and theories of mediation, and mediation advocacy. Class will include: 1) a concise overview of mediation approaches and theories, 2) skills exercises, 3) multiple mediation role plays, and 4) individualized video review. Together these will allow students to think about, practice, and experiment with, the most effective approaches to mediation advocacy and mediation. Elements used in grading: Attendance, Class Participation, and Video Review.  In Autumn Quarter, this class will meet Saturday, October 24 (9:00AM-4:30PM) and Sunday, October 25 (9:00AM-3:00PM). This class is limited to 15 students. CONSENT APPLICATION: To apply for this course, students must complete a Consent Application Form available at SLS Registrar https://registrar.law.stanford.edu/. See Consent Application Form for instructions and submission deadline.
